1.
The accused Balkishan @ Lalit is facing trial for offences s. 420 Indian Penal Code, 1860.
{Hereinafter 'Ipc'}.
2. The present case was lodged on the complaint of one Omveer who stated that he is in the business of supply of jeans pant from New F-77, Raghubeer Nagar, Rajori Garden.

He claims that around 01.5-02 months prior to his complaint, the accused Balkishan @Lalit came to his shop and stated that he is also in the business of supply of jeans pant and asked the complainant to supply material State vs Balkishan @ Lalit on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3253904/
1 to him.
Complainant claims that he took material from various persons and supplied the accused 06 times in lieu of which the accused paid 04 times demand drafts and two times through cheques.

Complainant states that out of these he handed over three demand drafts and one cheque to other parties and when the same were presented for encashment, the bank informed that the demand drafts are stolen.
After this the accused tried to avoid the complainant with the complainant claiming that the supply of goods and handing over of cheque/draft was being done in Gandhi Nagar Area.

Complainant claims that he came to know that the accused is present at Mahaveer Chowk,
Ashok Gali, Gandhi Nagar and he immediately went to the spot and caught him with other traders.
Complainant has further alleged that whenever he used to take demand drafts/cheque from the accused, he used to take the signature of the accused on a slip mentioning the DD/cheque number.
As per the version of the complainant, the accused had given DD worth Rs. 1,25,000/- and cheques worth Rs. 2,19,000/-.
Hence, the present case.

3. On the written application of the complainant, Gandhi Nagar P.S. registered in relation to the above incident FIR no. 63/2008 on 20.03.2008 and, after investigation, submitted the charge sheet on 19.05.2008 against the accused.
Cognizance was taken on the same date with provisions of section 207 Code of Criminal Procedure 1973{hereinafter 'CrPC'} also being complied on 19.05.2008.
4. Charge u/s. 420 IPC was framed on 07.07.2010 and read over to the accused, in Hindi, to which he denied the incident and claimed to be tried.
5. The prosecution, in order to prove the case beyond all reasonable doubt, examined 14 witnesses.

APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE 21.
In criminal proceedings, the case of the prosecution must be proved beyond all reasonable doubt.
Suspicion, however strong, cannot take the place of reasonable doubt and an accused is innocent unless proved guilty.
(Raja Naykar v. State of Chattisgarh 2024 INSC 56).

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: With this backdrop, this Court will proceed to examine whether the prosecution has proved its case against the accused beyond all reasonable doubt.

22. The case against the accused is that between the months of January to March 2008, he cheated the complainant by handing over four demand drafts and two cheques in lieu of supply of ready-made garments knowing the same would not be encashed.
He has accordingly been charged of the offence U/s 420 IPC. Section. 420 I.P.C. provides the punishment for cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.

It states that whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy, the whole or any part of valuable security, or anything, which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be liable to be punished for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.

The offence of cheating has been defined in section 415 I.P.C. as an act of fraudulent or dishonest intention intended to induce a person and the person so deceived delivers any property to any person, or consents that any person shall retain any property, causing damage or harm to that person.

23. The essentials required to be proved for bringing home the charge u/s. 420 IPC, as held in N.
Raghavender v. State of A.P., (2021) 18 SCC 70, are as follows: -
It is paramount that in order to attract the provisions of Section 420 IPC, the prosecution has to not only prove that the accused has cheated someone but also that by doing so, he has dishonestly induced the person who is cheated to deliver State vs Balkishan @ Lalit on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3253904/
6 property.

sentences.text: There are, thus, three components of this offence i.e. (i) deception of any person, (ii) fraudulently or dishonestly inducing that person to deliver any property to any person, and (iii) mens rea of the accused at the time of making the inducement.
It goes without saying that for the offence of cheating, fraudulent and dishonest intention must exist from the inception when the promise or representation was made 24.

Hence, the prosecution must prove that (i) the accused had fraudulently/ dishonestly deceived the complainant; (ii) complainant was induced with dishonest intention for the delivery of any property or valuable security; and (iii) as a result of such an act, complainant has suffered some damage or injury.
25.
As regards the case at hand; in order to prove its case, the prosecution has examined 14 witnesses along-with documentary evidence.
The star witness is the complainant examined as PW-2.

This witness has stepped into the witness box and deposed that between January-March 2008, accused came to his shop six times and requested this witness to give garments (jeans pants)
against cash payment.
However, payment was made by the accused by demand draft and, on two occasions, by cheques.
However, upon attempt to encash the DD/cheques, they were found to be stolen.

During his examination in chief, this witness correctly identified the demand drafts i.e. Ex.
PW2/K DD No. 064664, PNB Mayapur, Ex. PW2/L DD No. 064665 PNB Mayapur, Ex. PW2/O xerox of DD No. 368230 SBI, Ex. PW2/Q DD No. 368222 SBI Kithore as well as the cheques i.e. no.
110167 Ex. PW2/R, no. 000343 Ex. PW2/T, which had been given by the accused to him while also producing the five bills qua the garments purchased by him and subsequently sold to the accused.
26. PW-02 was cross examined extensively and nothing untoward has come in his cross examination to doubt his veracity.
He has deposed that the goods were purchased from one Parvez Khan, among other suppliers, and were sold in Gandhi Nagar.
He has reiterated the version in his examination in chief about meeting the accused in January 2008, for the first time, and supplying goods to him in lieu of cheque issued by the accused.
He has also, upon cross examination, deposed that the cheque had been handed over to one M/s. Berry and Berry but the same was returned within 30 days.

Apart from minor omissions like not remembering the exact dates on which accused had visited the shop of the complainant or the mobile number of the accused or the exact quantity of goods supplied to the accused, the testimony of this witness has remained unshaken and trustworthy.

27. The claim of the complainant regarding handing over of cheques and demand draft to other parties is further corroborated from the testimony of PW-9 who has deposed that the complainant has come to his shop as he used to buy garments from this witness and in lieu of trading, he had handed over a cheque and demand draft for the approximate amount of Rs. 2 lacs.
However, upon presentation, the same was not encashed for the reasons mentioned in the reason slip.

The contention by the counsel of the accused that this witness has not identified the accused and hence no reliance can be placed upon his testimony is misplaced as the testimony of this witness is relevant and corroborative qua the averments of complainant that he had handed over the cheques/DD given by the accused to other parties which were dishonored.

It is not the case of the State vs Balkishan @ Lalit on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3253904/
7 prosecution that the demand draft/cheque had been handed over to the accused by this witness.

Similarly, PW-11 Wali Zama Khan has also stepped into witness box and corroborated the claim of the complainant about demand drafts being handed over by the complainant in lieu of supply of garments by this witness to the complainant.
He has further correctly identified the demand drafts as well as invoice (Ex. PW2/L) and has also correctly identified the accused.

The testimony of this witness also corroborates the claim of the complainant that the accused and complainant had entered into a transaction for purchase of garments by the accused from the complainant since he has categorically deposed that complainant had told this witness in the shop of this witness about the complainant wanting to sell jeans to the accused.

During cross examination, this witness has remained unshaken and except for minor inconsistencies regarding the quality of jeans, there is no reason to doubt the veracity of this witnesses' testimony.
28. The version of the complainant/PW-2 that the cheques which had been handed over by the accused were stolen is corroborated from the testimony of PW-1 Anand Kumar.

As observed above,
the complainant has stated in his examination-in-chief that cheque no. 000343 Ex. PW2/T, had been handed over by accused but the same was stolen.

PW-1 has also deposed that aforesaid cheque drawn on Kotak Mahindra Bank, dated 19.02.2008 for an amount of Rs. 2 lacs, was stolen after being handed over to one D.K. Tomar, agent of Agmotext Fabrics, Kanpur.
Like PW-2, this witness cross examined at length on behalf of accused.
His testimony has remained consistent during cross examination and there is no reason to disbelieve the same.

Even further, Mr. D.K. Tomar has also stepped into the witness box as PW-7 and has corroborated the version of PW-2 that on 19.02.2008,
he was handed over a cheque of Rs. 2 lacs by the proprietor of Agmotech Fabrics Limited which was kept in his bag which was stolen later on.
29. Infact the factum of accused handing over false/stolen DD is also duly proved form the testimony of PW-12 Ms. Neha Kandari, PNB.

The complainant PW-2 has deposed that accused had handed over, among other DD/cheques, DD no. 64664 Ex. PW2/K was never PNB Mayapur,
Haridwar.
This witness has not been cross- examined at all by the accused and hence there is no reason to doubt the testimony of this witness.

Hence, it stands proved that the accused had used Ex.
PW 2/K, knowing it to be a forged document.

At the cost of repetition, this is in addition to the stolen cheque bearing no. 000343, exhibited as Ex. PW2/T, in the testimony of PW-2 and duly proved to be stolen in light of the observations/findings made above in light of the testimony of prosecution witnesses.

30. The remaining version /deposition of PW-2 that on 20.03.2008, he apprehended the accused at Mahavir Chowk, Ashok Gali Gandhi Nagar stands corroborated from the testimony of PW-5 Chander Shekhar who has deposed that on hearing noise on 20.03.2008, at around 06.30-7.00 PM,
he came outside and saw accused and complainant quarreling with each other about the transaction of money while correctly identifying the accused.
This witness was cross examined and his testimony has remained coherent.
The testimony of this witness is relevant for corroborating the claim of the complainant that he had apprehended the accused at the aforesaid date and time.

31. Hence, it stands proved that the complainant was approached by the accused for purchase of goods (jeans pants) and in lieu of such purchase, the accused had handed over, among others, one State vs Balkishan @ Lalit on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3253904/
8 demand draft bearing no. 064664 and a cheque no. 000343 which the accused knew were stolen and forged, which has been duly proved by the testimony of PW-12 and PW-01, respectively.
By handing over such forged and stolen Demand draft and cheque, he deceived the complainant to deliver garments to him and thereby causing financial damage to the complainant.
Accused has not led any DE nor has he been able punch holes in the case of the prosecution.
Rather the testimony and overall evidence led by the prosecution has remained cogent and trustworthy and also been corroborated in material aspects.
The charge u/s 420 IPC has been proved beyond all reasonable doubt against the accused by the prosecution.
DECISION 32.In light of the aforesaid discussion
, this Court is of the considered opinion that the prosecution has proved its case, against all reasonable doubt against the prosecution.
33.The accused Balkishan @ Lalit s/o Late Sh. Moti Ram is hereby convicted of the offence punishable under Section 420 IPC.
34.Copy of this judgment be given free of cost to the convict.
35.Let the convict be heard separately on the aspect of sentence.

The accused Balkishan @ Lalit is facing trial for offences s. 420 Indian Penal Code, 1860.
2. The present case was lodged on the complaint of one Omveer who stated that he is in the business of supply of jeans pant from New F-77, Raghubeer Nagar, Rajori Garden.
He claims that around 01.5-02 months prior to his complaint, the accused Balkishan @Lalit came to his shop and stated that he is also in the business of supply of jeans pant and asked the complainant to supply material State vs Balkishan @ Lalit on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3253904/
1 to him.

Complainant states that out of these he handed over three demand drafts and one cheque to other parties and when the same were presented for encashment, the bank informed that the demand drafts are stolen.
After this the accused tried to avoid the complainant with the complainant claiming that the supply of goods and handing over of cheque/draft was being done in Gandhi Nagar Area.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE 21.
In criminal proceedings, the case of the prosecution must be proved beyond all reasonable doubt.
Suspicion, however strong, cannot take the place of reasonable doubt and an accused is innocent unless proved guilty.
(Raja Naykar v. State of Chattisgarh 2024 INSC 56).
He has accordingly been charged of the offence U/s 420 IPC. Section. 420 I.P.C. provides the punishment for cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.
23. The essentials required to be proved for bringing home the charge u/s. 420 IPC, as held in N.
Raghavender v. State of A.P., (2021) 18 SCC 70, are as follows: -
It is paramount that in order to attract the provisions of Section 420 IPC, the prosecution has to not only prove that the accused has cheated someone but also that by doing so, he has dishonestly induced the person who is cheated to deliver State vs Balkishan @ Lalit on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3253904/
6 property.
There are, thus, three components of this offence i.e. (i) deception of any person, (ii) fraudulently or dishonestly inducing that person to deliver any property to any person, and (iii) mens rea of the accused at the time of making the inducement.
It goes without saying that for the offence of cheating, fraudulent and dishonest intention must exist from the inception when the promise or representation was made 24.
Hence, the prosecution must prove that (i) the accused had fraudulently/ dishonestly deceived the complainant; (ii) complainant was induced with dishonest intention for the delivery of any property or valuable security; and (iii) as a result of such an act, complainant has suffered some damage or injury.
25.
31. Hence, it stands proved that the complainant was approached by the accused for purchase of goods (jeans pants) and in lieu of such purchase, the accused had handed over, among others, one State vs Balkishan @ Lalit on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3253904/
8 demand draft bearing no. 064664 and a cheque no. 000343 which the accused knew were stolen and forged, which has been duly proved by the testimony of PW-12 and PW-01, respectively.
By handing over such forged and stolen Demand draft and cheque, he deceived the complainant to deliver garments to him and thereby causing financial damage to the complainant.
Accused has not led any DE nor has he been able punch holes in the case of the prosecution.
Rather the testimony and overall evidence led by the prosecution has remained cogent and trustworthy and also been corroborated in material aspects.
The charge u/s 420 IPC has been proved beyond all reasonable doubt against the accused by the prosecution.
, this Court is of the considered opinion that the prosecution has proved its case, against all reasonable doubt against the prosecution.
